papers.title: Cryo-EM structures of an Acinetobacter baumannii podovirus reveal a canonical capsid maturation
papers.abstract: Phages that hunting multidrug resistant bacteria represent a promising approach in precision medicine nowadays, including these infecting Acinetobacter baumannii. To data, a large number of A. baumannii phages has been isolated, however, complete structural information remains not adequately released. Previously, we reported a podovirus, AbP20, that infects A. baumannii with potent efficacy in mouse model. In the present work, we further report the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of AbP20 and its procapsid. The near-atomic resolution reveals that AbP20 is composed of five distinct structural subunits, i.e., capsid, portal, nozzle, fiber, and adaptor. We then characterized the assembly mechanisms of molecular interactions within capsid and portal-tail complex. By co-expressing the scaffold protein and the capsid protein of AbP20, we constructed the self-assembled DNA-free procapsid of AbP20. A near-atomic resolution reconstruction reveals it a double-layered concentric spherical architecture with a nearly 1:1 ratio of these two proteins. Comparison between the mature and apo-form of the capsid of AbP20 uncovers a canonical model of conformational switch from procapsid to capsid. Altogether, the present work reports the first whole atom structure of a podovirus infecting A. baumannii, providing a reference for structure-based phage engineering and editing.

papers.title: Identification and characterization of new P. aeruginosa phages using a surface receptor platform
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages are of increasing interest for their potential use as alternatives to antibiotics for treating drug-resistant infections. Phage steering, specifically receptor-based steering, involves use of phages that bias the development of resistance in bacteria towards phenotypes such as reduced fitness. Phage therapy typically involves administering cocktails of phages with different targets to reduce the likelihood of resistance emerging. To ensure effective steering and cocktail design, there is a need to identify the receptors used by phages of interest, and to isolate phages that use diverse receptors. Here we describe a SURFAce Receptor (SURFAR) platform consisting of a set of defined Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains and mutants for rapid characterization of phage receptors. This platform can also be used to enrich for and isolate diverse phages from environmental samples, yielding novel phage genomes from wastewater. Using the SURFAR platform, two new phages were isolated and characterized: Dalewood, which targets both flagella and the conserved LPS outer core, and Bowman, a biofilm targeting phage capable of supressing growth of a subset of carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates. This tool helps to standardize the laborious but important task of phage receptor characterization, with the goal of expanding the known repertoire of P. aeruginosa phage receptors and phages.

papers.title: Magnetic organelle gene clusters enable bacterial growth and ATP homeostasis under oxidizing conditions
papers.abstract: Biological organisms can produce magnetic nanoparticles made of magnetite to detect the Earth's magnetic field for orientation. The evolutionary mechanisms that led to the acquisition of this capacity remain unknown. The most ancient organisms known to perform magnetic orientation are magnetotactic bacteria. Under tight genetic control, they produce chains of magnetite nanoparticles in dedicated organelles to allow efficient navigation in aquatic environments containing molecular oxygen. Yet, these bacteria have been proposed to emerge before molecular oxygen became abundant on Earth, at a time when this navigation system could not have served its current function. Here, we show that gene clusters responsible of magnetite formation and organization enable resistance against hydrogen peroxide, a toxic oxygen-derived compound that was produced during the early stages of Earth's oxygenation when iron oxidation consumed molecular oxygen. Characterization of the nanoparticle's oxidation state supported the involvement of magnetite in resistance to hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress. These findings are compatible with an early emergence of magnetotactic bacteria, before natural waters became oxygenated. We propose a conceptual framework to explain the origin of magnetic orientation in bacteria, and offer tools to identify the initiation of Earth's oxygenation in a time-resolved manner.

papers.title: Microbially conjugated bile acids differentially affect the lifecycle and pathogenesis of Clostridioides difficile
papers.abstract: Clostridioides difficile is a Gram-positive bacterium that causes C. difficile infection (CDI). In healthy adults, it has been proposed that the gut microbiota provides colonization resistance against C. difficile by competition through nutrient limitation and antagonism through secondary bile acid metabolism, the latter of which is mediated by the deconjugation of host-derived bile acids with bacterial bile salt hydrolases (BSH). Recently, BSHs have also shown an ability to reconjugate non-canonical (i.e., not glycine or taurine) amino acids to sterol cores, resulting in novel microbially conjugated bile acids (MCBAs). MCBAs have been associated with the resolution of recurrent CDI, though the mechanism underlying these effects are not well understood. To address this gap, we synthesized 36 MCBAs with nine amino acids (cysteine, isoleucine, leucine, phenylalanine, proline, serine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and valine) conjugated to the primary and secondary bile acids found in the human gut (CA, DCA, CDCA, and LCA) and tested their impact on various stages of C. difficiles lifecycle including bacterial outgrowth, membrane integrity, sporulation, and toxin activity. We show that BSH-mediated amidation of bile acid sterol cores can either increase or decrease inhibitory effects on C. difficile in an amino acid-dependent manner. For example, serine MCBAs enhanced C. difficiles ability to grow in otherwise inhibitory bile acid concentrations, increased spore production, and elevated toxin activity. Tryptophan MCBAs increased inhibition. By demonstrating these variable effects, our work clarifies the molecular determinants of MCBA activity and highlights specific MCBAs as promising targets for the development of C. difficile microbial-based therapeutics.

papers.title: Citrobacter rodentium infection disrupts colonic mucus barrier function via ablation of intercrypt goblet cells
papers.abstract: The colonic mucus barrier, composed of distinct layers maintained by specialized goblet cell (GC) subtypes, forms the first line of defense against enteric pathogens. However, the individual contributions of inner (IML) and fecal (FML) mucus layers to barrier integrity, and how these layers and the GC responses are dynamically modulated during infection remain incompletely understood. Using Citrobacter rodentium infection in mice, we show that early colonization disrupts the inner mucus layer, increases mucus penetrability and drives alterations in faecal mucus layer thickness. Spatial imaging revealed progressive crypt infiltration and concurrent accumulation of pathogen clusters within the FML. Transcriptomic and functional analyses identified Spdef-dependent intercrypt goblet cells (icGCs) as essential for sustaining IML integrity and limiting epithelial access. Spdef-deficient mice exhibited delayed clearance and enhanced crypt invasion, highlighting the protective role of icGCs. Infection selectively depleted icGCs, collapsing the intercrypt mucus and creating permissive niches for colonization. Mechanistically, C. rodentium leveraged its type III secretion system, specifically the EspF effector to reprogram GC transcriptional responses, inducing metabolic stress and promoting apoptotic signatures in GCs specifically. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized virulence strategy in which EspF-driven GC remodeling compromises intercrypt mucus defenses, potentially facilitating pathogen persistence and transmission.

papers.title: The MarR-family regulator TilR links biosynthesis of enterotoxin tilimycin with physiologic adaptation in Klebsiella oxytoca
papers.abstract: Members of the Klebsiella oxytoca species complex (KoSC) are ubiquitous gut colonizers that produce the DNA-damaging enterotoxin tilimycin (TM) as part of their virulence-related program. A MarR-like transcriptional regulator, herein designated TilR, controls expression of the divergently transcribed aroX- and NRPS-operons responsible for TM production. Deletion of tilR resulted in pronounced induction of both operons, elevated toxin production, and increased cytotoxicity - establishing TilR as the key repressor of TM biosynthesis. TilR is encoded downstream of the NRPS operon and binds a 20 bp motif within the aroX-NRPS intergenic region, spatially separated from the predicted promoters driving toxin gene expression. Analysis of global transcriptome profiles revealed that TilR, the most highly expressed of the seven MarRs in KoSC, links toxin biosynthesis to a broader transcriptional network involved in nutrient acquisition, stress adaptation, and central metabolism. In addition, TM production coincided with induction of multiple virulence-associated genes involved in adhesion, biofilm formation, and iron acquisition. Phylogenetic and structural analyses revealed that TilR is distinct from canonical MarRs and absent from members of the closely related, competing Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC). These findings identify TilR as an evolutionarily specialized global regulator that coordinates TM biosynthesis with broader metabolic, stress-adaptive, and virulence-associated transcriptional responses.

papers.title: Starve, stress, and mate: Activation of the CCAAT-Binding complex overrides sterility of mating-type heterozygous Candida albicans
papers.abstract: Sexual reproduction in the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans is typically restricted by a strict genetic lock: the a1-2 repressor present in standard mating-type heterozygous (MTLa/) diploid strains, which actively represses mating competency. While severe environmental pressures are known to influence fungal development, the molecular mechanisms that allow cells to override this genetic sterility block remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the highly conserved CCAAT-binding complex (CBC) as the critical developmental hub that integrates environmental stress to unlock mating in heterozygous diploids. By combining proteomic mapping (ChIP-SICAP) and transcriptomics (RNA-Seq) to define the regulatory network of the core CBC subunit Hap5, we demonstrate that CBC hyperactivation completely overrides the a1-2 repressor. This activation triggers a robust white-to-opaque phenotypic switch and initiates a mating-competence program in MTLa/ strains genetically locked in a sterile state. Crucially, this developmental transition is antagonized by the iron-regulatory partner Hap43, but is strictly dependent on physical interaction at the chromatin level with Cap1, the master regulator of the oxidative stress response. Our findings reveal that the CBC and Cap1 couple metabolic starvation (glucose and iron limitation) and oxidative stress to a core reproductive program, providing a mechanistic basis for how C. albicans bypasses genetic constraints on sexual reproduction to generate genetic diversity under hostile host conditions.

papers.title: Asymmetric division and polar growth define a non-canonical cell cycle in Bradyrhizobium.
papers.abstract: Bradyrhizobia are widely used as plant growth promoters in agriculture, yet their cell biology remains poorly understood. Here, we described for the first time, nucleoid segregation dynamics and the cell cycle of Bradyrhizobium at the cellular level. We show that highly asymmetric polar growth generates a short daughter cell and a longer mother cell at each division. Nucleoid compaction and positioning change across growth phases, culminating in a highly compacted, asymmetrically positioned nucleoid in stationary phase. ParB presents a subpolar localization, at the nucleoid periphery. Despite this pronounced cellular asymmetry and the presence of a single large chromosome, chromosome conformation capture reveals a global chromosome organization similar to that of bacteria undergoing conventional binary fission Together, these findings uncover a distinctive cell cycle program in Bradyrhizobium. showing that such extreme asymmetry in growth and division, significantly different from closely related characterized -Proteobacteriota, is compatible with conserved principles of chromosome organization.

papers.title: Decoding the molecular cues regulating the transition of Influenza virus polymerase from transcriptase to replicase.
papers.abstract: Influenza virus polymerase (FluPol) dynamically transitions between distinct conformational states to coordinate viral gene transcription and genome replication. While vRNP-associated monomeric FluPol supports transcription, ANP32-dependent asymmetric and ANP32-independent symmetric polymerase dimers mediate genome and antigenome (vRNA/cRNA) replication. How FluPol coordinates these distinct functional states to maintain the transcription-replication balance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize interdomain interactions within PB2 that govern the stability of the replication-competent conformation of FluPol. Specifically, a highly conserved salt bridge between PB2 Mid-E282 and NLS-K752 stabilizes the replicase conformation, while the charge state of residue 627 (E or K) dictates ANP32 engagement, together coordinating polymerase dimerization and replication activity. Strikingly, bat influenza A viruses H17N10 and H18N11 harbor unconventional serine substitutions at both positions, compromising polymerase dimerization, ANP32 interaction, and vRNA/cRNA replication. Remarkably, introducing these bat-signature substitutions (E282S/K627S) into human H1N1 polymerase results in phosphorylation at both positions in human cells. These findings suggest that phosphorylation can partially compensate for the loss of negative charge at these residues, revealing a phosphomimetic adaptation mechanism that modulates polymerase conformational dynamics and function. Collectively, our study reveals how a conserved interdomain interaction within PB2 regulates conformational transitions and transcription-replication balance of FluPol, which might have been driven by phosphomimetic adaptations during the course of a diverse range of influenza virus evolution.

papers.title: Genomic analysis of the Streptococcus anginosus group; taxonomic implications, evolutionary insights and clinical considerations
papers.abstract: Background: The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) (S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group's diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods: Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results: Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa (S. anginosus, S. hominis, S. whileyi and S. vaginalis). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex-S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ~15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity (S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions: Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.

papers.title: LAP-TLR2 Axis Drives Inflammatory Pathology during Listeria monocytogenes Gastroenteritis
papers.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) causes acute gastroenteritis that precedes systemic invasive listeriosis, yet the molecular mechanisms coordinating bacterial virulence with host inflammatory responses during the enteric phase remain poorly understood. We show that Lm-associated gastroenteritis is dose-dependent, and a high infectious dose (~1x10^10 CFU/mouse), reflecting epidemic cases, recapitulates hallmark features of gastroenteritis in a mouse model, including early onset, epithelial erosion, and profound inflammatory cell infiltration. We identify Listeria adhesion protein (LAP), rather than classical virulence factors such as internalin A and listeriolysin O, as the primary mediator of enteric pathology, driving epithelial cell death and neutrophil recruitment. Transcriptomic (mRNA-seq) profiling implicates LAP-driven engagement of the TLR2-MyD88 pathway. Using the HEK-Dual hTLR2 (NF-kB) reporter cell line and TLR2 knockout mice, we show that LAP engages TLR2 to activate TNFalpha; NF-kB signaling and compromises the gut epithelial barrier. Disease severity correlates with myeloid hyperactivation and intestinal ion channel dysregulation, as CD11b-; mice exhibit attenuated diarrhea despite elevated bacterial tissue loads. Finally, studies in MLCK knock-out mice confirm that this myeloid-driven pathology requires MLCK-dependent tight junction opening for paracellular neutrophil migration, which works in concert with LAP-TLR2 signaling during Lm-induced gastroenteritis.

papers.title: Metabolites cross the membrane, the transcriptome does not follow: co-localization is required for the cyanobacterial response to a yeast partner
papers.abstract: Interactions between phototrophs and heterotrophs are usually explained by cross-feeding, yet whether that exchange alone accounts for the phototroph's response has rarely been tested. We grew the sucrose-secreting cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus with the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides as a synthetic community, either in mixed co-culture or in membrane-separated co-culture (0.22 m pore size), each with a matched axenic control. Metabolite exchange occurred in both configurations: sucrose reached the yeast and was consumed, and yeast-derived metabolites reached the cyanobacterium. The yeast reached a higher final density behind the membrane, whereas the cyanobacterium gained about 9% over its axenic control only in mixed co-culture. Yet the cyanobacterial transcriptome responded only with co-localization: expression of 51 genes changed consistently across time points (day-averaged q < 0.05), against one gene behind the membrane, and the number of differentially expressed genes rose from 20 on day 4 to 91 and 127 on days 6 and 8. Nine regulatory programs (iModulons), mainly nitrogen and photosynthesis, responded in mixed co-culture and none behind the membrane. Reactor configuration alone changed 40 genes in axenic culture. These results suggest that co-localization, in addition to metabolite exchange, was required for the heterotrophic partner to trigger a response in the phototroph. Co-culture studies that infer interactions from shared metabolites may miss effects that depend on spatial structure. Importance Partnerships between light-powered microbes and the heterotrophs living alongside them move large amounts of carbon in oceans and soils, and are now built on purpose to turn carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals. Such partnerships are usually described by the chemicals the partners trade, so we asked whether those chemicals are enough. The cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus and the yeast Rhodotorula toruloides were grown together in one vessel, or in two chambers divided by a membrane that molecules cross but cells cannot. The yeast fed on cyanobacterial sugar in both, yet the cyanobacterium changed its gene activity only when the two shared a space. Partners in nature are usually clustered rather than evenly mixed, so closeness may contribute as much as the chemicals themselves. Keeping partners apart in engineered cultures can still deliver carbon to the heterotroph, but may not deliver the benefits of partnership to the phototroph.

papers.title: The enemy of my enemy: A bacterial antagonist rescues Chlamydomonas by inactivating a toxin from a rival
papers.abstract: Microbial interactions are shaped by multiple community members, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a tripartite interaction between the microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and two Pseudomonas bacteria that coexist in the same soil habitat. In pairwise cultures, all three interactions are amensalistic (-like): Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5 antagonizes both C. reinhardtii and Pseudomonas fluorescens HKI0770 without benefit, while P. fluorescens inhibits C. reinhardtii without profiting from the alga. However, in a tripartite culture, P. fluorescens protects C. reinhardtii from P. protegens and promotes algal recovery. This protection is not stopped when the used carbon source, acetate, is supplemented. The P. fluorescens rescue effect is associated with reduced levels of the polyyne toxin protegencin produced by P. protegens. Protegencin levels, detected by Raman microspectroscopy, are decreased by application of spent medium or protein extracts from P. fluorescens, while heat- and protease-treatment abolish this activity. A heat-sensitive, proteinaceous factor, likely an enzyme(s), appears to contribute to protegencin inactivation. Our results show that P. fluorescens rescues C. reinhardtii by inactivating protegencin, despite being inhibited by P. protegens. These findings demonstrate the importance of investigating higher-order effects, since additional community members can transform pairwise antagonistic interactions into conditional protection through toxin inactivation.

papers.title: Integrative identification of Tetratostichococcus sp. CCAH0201 (Trebouxiophyceae, Chlorophyta) from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam
papers.abstract: A microalgal strain from Rhizophora leaves in the Can Gio Mangrove Forest, Vietnam, was examined by light microscopy and three molecular markers. Thirty-six cells from 22 micrographs measured 6.68-12.74 by 3.49-4.79 micrometres. Homologous phylogenetic windows comprised 550 nucleotides for SSU rDNA, 711 for ITS and 1,170 for rbcL. CCAH0201, P1 and Tetratostichococcus jenerensis SAG 2138 shared the SSU 3-prime sequence, whereas ITS and rbcL placed CCAH0201 with P1 (SH-aLRT/UFBoot 87/94 and 96.9/99). CCAH0201 differed from P1 at 22/711 ITS and 4/1,170 rbcL sites. Structure-guided ITS2 comparison identified one strict CBC, one two-sided change from a wobble pair and three hemi-CBCs relative to P1. CCAH0201 is thus identified as Tetratostichococcus sp. in a lineage close to P1.

papers.title: CauloBrowser 2.0: an AI powered update
papers.abstract: CauloBrowser is a systems-biology database for Caulobacter crescentus that organizes the largest repository of experimental data for this model bacterium. The original CauloBrowser provided a web interface for accessing these data, but the growing number of experimental datasets and advances in AI chatbots motivated an updated resource. We developed CauloBrowser 2.0 (CauloBrowser.org) as an open-source application that broadens access to RNA-seq, microarray, ribosome profiling, Tn-seq, ChIP-seq, and genome annotation data. The CauloChat AI interface allows users to query these datasets in natural language, generate visualizations, and achieve complex biological insights. While the database is hosted freely on the web, users may also download the database and run it locally, reducing dependence on the web-hosted service and allowing laboratories to use compatible unpublished datasets. Altogether, CauloBrowser 2.0 provides a significant update for exploring diverse systems biology data in C. crescentus.

papers.title: Metatranscriptomic Profiling of Viral Diversity in Aquatic Environments with a Focus on Microalgal Viruses
papers.abstract: Freshwater microeukaryotes contribute to aquatic productivity, yet the RNA viruses associated with these communities remain incompletely characterized compared with their marine counterparts. Here, we used metatranscriptomics to profile viral diversity across five Finnish freshwater sites (one river and four lakes) and one coastal marine sample from Hiroshima Bay in the Seto Inland Sea, Japan. We recovered 399 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), of which 285 (71.4%) represented RNA viruses distributed across five viral phyla and putatively associated with fungal, plant or algal, metazoan and bacterial hosts. DNA viruses formed a smaller component of the dataset, including bacteriophage-like vOTUs with transcripts encoding replication, structural, packaging, and lysis proteins. Two vOTUs, which were detected in the Vantaanjoki river sample, were putatively classified within the family Marnaviridae, which comprises RNA viruses that infect protists in marine and freshwater environments. Both vOTUs encoded conserved replication and picornavirus-like capsid domains, and one represented a near-complete dicistronic genome. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) -based phylogeny placed these vOTUs in a strongly supported lineage outside the currently recognized genera within the family Marnaviridae, supporting their provisional assignment to the candidate genus Vandarnavirus proposed here within Marnaviridae. Whole-genome comparisons using the IMG/VR v4 database revealed genetic similarities between the vOTUs representing the candidate Vandarnavirus genus and picorna-like virus sequences from freshwater, wetland, saltmarsh, and estuarine metatranscriptomes. These findings expand the known ecological range of marnavirus-like RNA viruses and identify freshwater habitats as under-sampled reservoirs of microalgae-associated viral sequences.

papers.title: Evaluating non-oxidative glycolysis using 13C metabolic flux analysis
papers.abstract: Non-oxidative glycolysis (NOG) converts glucose to acetyl-CoA without emitting CO2 during Escherichia coli bioproduction. Although 13C-metabolic flux analysis (13C-MFA) has the potential to evaluate NOG flux distribution in vivo, the precision of these estimates depends on the labeling patterns of glucose tracers. Because E. coli has multiple native glycolysis pathways, selecting the optimal glucose tracer is important for precise estimates. This study used simulations to evaluate the performance of 18 commercially available glucose tracers in precisely predicting NOG flux. We artificially generated flux distributions of central metabolic pathways, including three types of NOG pathways, and obtained 13C labeling patterns of amino acids metabolized from each glucose tracer. Using these data, we then calculated 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for NOG pathway fluxes. Comparing the sum of CI widths from three NOG fluxes showed that estimation with [1,3-13C]-glucose yielded the narrowest CIs. Several tracers, including [2,3-13C]glucose, were capable of determining fluxes with high precision, but [1-13C]glucose was not one of them, despite often being used for estimating glycolytic fluxes. We then experimentally evaluated [2,3-13C]- and [1-13C]glucose as tracers in E. coli strains with and without the expression of phosphoketolase, which is required for NOG pathways to function. The results suggested that [1-13C]glucose could not detect NOG fluxes, whereas [2,3-13C]glucose estimated the fluxes of all three NOG pathways with narrow CIs.

papers.title: Visual surfaceomics reveals the substrate-scavenging cell surface of Asgard archaea
papers.abstract: The emergence of eukaryotes from Asgard archaeal ancestors likely required a specialized cell envelope that enabled sustained physical and metabolic interactions with proto-mitochondrial symbionts. While the protrusion-rich cell architecture of Asgard archaea may enable such interactions, the molecular composition of their cell surface and its role in establishing cell-cell contacts remains unknown. Here, we developed a "visual surfaceomics" approach, integrating subtomogram averaging, predictive structural modeling, transcriptomics, proteomics, and expansion microscopy to identify surface proteins in situ. We show that Asgard cell bodies and protrusions lack an archaea-typical paracrystalline S-layer and are instead decorated by two main classes of surface proteins: subtilisin-like serine proteases (SubSs) and oligopeptide-binding proteins (OppAs). SubSs were detected as membrane-anchored dimers and were sparsely distributed across the surface. OppAs showed near-total membrane coverage but lacked any rigid, higher order assembly. Thermal shift assays and single particle cryo-EM showed that OppA binds oligopeptides in vitro. Comparative genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics suggest that this peptidophilic surface architecture is conserved across Asgard archaeal phyla. Finally, we discovered that the cell surface was remodeled at cell-cell contact sites. Altogether, our integrative approach revealed a metabolically specialized and structurally flexible cell surface that couples extracellular protein degradation with peptide capture and uptake, while potentially contributing to establishing and maintaining the symbiotic interactions of Asgard archaea.

papers.title: Genomic signatures distinguish isolates of Salmonella Typhimurium from humans and livestock
papers.abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium is a major cause of human salmonellosis and livestock represent an important reservoir for human infection through the food chain. However, it remains unclear whether isolates recovered from human disease reflect the broader livestock population or constitute a subset of livestock-associated isolates characterized by specific genetic features. Here, we analysed 1,398 S. Typhimurium genomes from human, poultry, bovine and swine isolates to evaluate whether isolates associated with human disease can be distinguished from those circulating in livestock and to identify the genetic features underlying this discrimination. Whole-genome multilocus sequence typing profiles were converted into a gene presence/absence matrix and analysed using four machine-learning algorithms, which showed high and consistent discriminatory performance. Model performance was influenced by the phylogenetic structure of the population and by the variable distribution of human- and livestock-associated isolates across lineages of sequence type (ST) 19, the most prevalent S. Typhimurium ST. Nevertheless, within ST19, 97 genes were significantly enriched and 36 were significantly depleted in human-associated genomes relative to genomes from each of the three livestock sources. Human-enriched genes included 14 genes required for biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide core, the O-antigen, the T1 antigen, and six virulence factors. These genes were consistently absent from livestock-associated genomes across ST19 lineages. Conversely, human-depleted genes included the galactitol utilisation cluster and five virulence genes, which are predominantly absent in specific ST19 lineages. Overall, our findings support the existence of host-associated genomic signatures that distinguish isolates associated with human disease from those sampled from the livestock reservoir.

papers.title: UVC Irradiation Induces Time-Dependent Proteomic Remodeling in Geodermatophilus obscurus G20
papers.abstract: Geodermatophilus obscurus G20 is a multi-resistant extremophile observed to survive significant dosages of ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Despite previous work having measured G. obscurus G20s proteome in relation to its genome sequence, its proteomic response to stressors has yet to be explored. This study utilizes bottom-up proteomics with data independent acquisition to derive comprehensive proteomic measurements in both healthy and two UV-stressed conditions induced through 254 nm UV radiation administered at a median lethal dose. The first, an acute response treatment group, was recovered and flash-frozen immediately after UV radiation. The second, a recovery response treatment group, was allowed to incubate for 1 hour following UV radiation. Gene enrichment analysis revealed an increase in NADH dehydrogenase activity among both stressed treatment groups, however the recovery response treatment group experienced additional changes including reduced peptidoglycan synthesis and increased translational activity. Results suggest that the repair process undergone by G. obscurus G20 persists well after initial UV exposure and is likely to be inducing noteworthy energetic demands to facilitate UV induced genomic repair. Proteomic analyses revealed patterns that advance our mechanistic and temporal understanding of the G. obscurus metabolic response to UV irradiation.

papers.title: The biochemical composition of coronavirus Nucleocapsid proteins drives the bicistronic properties of their sub-genomic mRNAs
papers.abstract: The nucleocapsid (N) gene of coronaviruses (CoVs) encodes a structural RNA-binding protein required for viral assembly. In SARS- and MERS-CoV viruses, reading frame 2 of N contains an overlapping open reading frame (ORF) encoding an innate immune antagonist accessory protein. However, the extent of this dual coding capacity across the CoV family, and the genetic features driving overlapping ORF formation, remain unexamined. Here, we developed an in-silico tool (ORFan) to screen structural gene sub-genomic mRNA sequences from 152 species of coronavirus for the presence of overlapping accessory gene candidates. We found that frame 2 of the N gene in Alpha-, Beta- and Delta-CoVs frequently contains a potential accessory ORF (AcORF), conserved at the subgenus level, unlike the spike, envelope and membrane genes. We also show that CoV nucleotide biases in conjunction with codon biases integral to N protein function drive the relatively high abundances of start codons in frame two and stop codons in frame three, explaining the tendency towards frame 2 AcORFs. We further suggest that viral nucleotide biases and the codon composition required for RNA-binding function facilitate overlapping ORF formation in other virus families

papers.title: Cell-scale confinement reorders bacterial speed rankings
papers.abstract: Which bacterium swims fastest depends on where the race is run. Speeds are usually measured in open liquid, yet many bacteria live in pores, mucus and host passages no wider than a cell. Using a microfluidic device with eight channel widths (0.80-3.00 m) in one field of view, we tracked unlabeled cells of eight species spanning five motility systems. Chamber height, a polymer additive and channel width each reordered the ranking. Vibrio alginolyticus, the fastest in open liquid, slowed to ~4 m/s in 1.25-m channels, whereas Campylobacter jejuni and Bacillus subtilis kept 33-46 m/s. Open liquid speed did not predict robustness to confinement. In two unrelated lineages, host symbionts that pass through narrow passages during colonization, Caballeronia insecticola and Vibrio fischeri, outran their non-symbiotic relatives in the channels, and crossed them with flagella wrapped around the cell body at nearly the speed of unwrapped cells. Where space is tight, the ability to keep moving, not top speed, sets the ranking.

papers.title: High reproducibility demonstrated in a direct-to-consumer microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions using fecal reference material
papers.abstract: Recent studies have documented substantial variation in microbiome profiles recovered from identical biological samples across direct-to-consumer (DTC) gut microbiome testing providers and, in some cases, within individual providers. These reports underscore the need for transparent, published assessments of analytical performance from the companies offering these services. To assess analytical reproducibility in our own testing workflow, we processed 10 replicates of a homogenized National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) human fecal reference material (RM 8048) through our full sample processing pipeline, from sample collection to data generation. Replicates were shipped from five U.S. sites over a staggered 35-day window. They were processed amongst over 6,000 customer samples, batched for DNA extraction and sequencing based on their arrival in the lab in nine separate sequencing runs, and analyzed using our standard pipeline. The 10 reference material replicates yielded highly concordant community profiles regardless of shipping time or temperature. Technical variability was minimal (median Bray-Curtis dissimilarity = 0.04) compared with the variation observed in samples from the same Tiny Health customer collected the same day (median Bray-Curtis: 0.08), within one week (0.25), one to two weeks apart (0.28), and between unrelated individuals (0.88). When evaluated using NIST's Coefficient of Disagreement (COD) metric, our workflow yielded a maximum pairwise COD of 0.045, well below NIST's published upper bound of 0.073 for this reference material. All three spike-in control strains were successfully recovered from every sample. These results demonstrate the reproducibility of our DTC microbiome testing workflow under real-world conditions, with robust consistency across sample collection, shipping, laboratory processing, and bioinformatics analysis. They also highlight the value of RM 8048 and similar reference materials for evaluating and transparently reporting analytical performance in DTC microbiome testing.

papers.title: Dynamic allocation of MurJ coordinates bacterial growth and division
papers.abstract: Rod-shaped bacteria grow by inserting peptidoglycan into the lateral cell wall during elongation and into the septal cell wall during division. These two modes of growth are driven by distinct peptidoglycan synthesis machineries that consume the shared precursor Lipid II and must be coordinated so that cell enlargement remains matched to division. However, how cells spatially allocate this shared precursor, and whether Lipid II translocation itself contributes to this coordi-nation, remain unclear. Here we show that the spatial distribution of the essential Lipid II flippase MurJ coordinates this balance in Escherichia coli. Increasing nonseptal MurJ abundance shifted cell-wall synthesis toward elongation and reduced septal synthesis. Single-molecule tracking revealed that MurJ diffuses throughout the membrane but is transiently captured at the division site, rather than stably incorporated into the septal synthesis machinery. This recruitment requires active septal cell-wall synthesis, but not ongoing Lipid II synthesis or flipping, indicating that MurJ recruitment is coupled to the active synthesis machinery rather than to substrate availability or transport. Thus, activation of septal synthesis creates transient MurJ capture at the division site, providing a mechanism to preferentially supply Lipid II for septal growth during cytokinesis. These findings reveal a capture-and-release mechanism that dynamically enriches MurJ at active division sites and thereby coordinates elongation and division in bacterial cells.

papers.title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates
papers.abstract: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous {beta}-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.

papers.title: A Urinary Metabolomic Signature Associated with Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Children with Short Bowel Syndrome
papers.abstract: Direct sampling of the small intestinal microbiome is challenging. Urinary metabolites may offer a noninvasive approach to studying microbial functional activity. We used clinically available gas chromatography/mass spectrometry to profile urinary organic acids in 94 children with short bowel syndrome, comparing those with clinically defined small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO; n=21) with those without SIBO (n=73). SIBO-associated metabolites included microbial fermentation products, dietary derivatives, and host metabolic intermediates. Metabolites enriched in SIBO mapped to aromatic amino acid metabolism, including tryptophan and tyrosine pathways, consistent with altered microbial fermentation. Many associations persisted after adjustment for intestinal anatomy, age, antibiotic exposure, and nutritional composition. These findings identified a urinary metabolic profile associated with clinically defined SIBO in children with short bowel syndrome and support further evaluation of urinary metabolomics as a noninvasive approach to studying small intestinal microbial function.

papers.title: Second-site capsule-locus mutations, not Ade efflux disruption, determine phage susceptibility across an Acinetobacter baumannii transposon mutant panel
papers.abstract: Resistance-Nodulation-Division (RND) efflux pumps have been implicated in phage adsorption in several Gram-negative bacteria, suggesting that AdeABC, AdeFGH and AdeIJK, the three characterised RND efflux systems of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, could play a similar role. We tested this hypothesis using five phages (Equilibrator, Taro, AT01, BB02, and AC03) and a panel of 13 A. baumannii strains, including nine AB5075 transposon mutants affecting AdeABC, AdeFGH, or AdeIJK. Host-range testing, efficiency-of-plating assays, capsule-associated density measurements, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing were performed to assess the relationship between genotype and phage infection. Overall, the data did not support a role for the Ade components as receptors. Phages Equilibrator, Taro and AT01 formed plaques on every strain, and the restricted host ranges of BB02 and AC03 did not correspond to disruption of a particular efflux system. Sequencing instead identified second-site mutations in the KL25 capsule locus in six of the ten AB5075 strains. These included a 1,998-bp deletion affecting wzc, substitutions in mnaA and mnaB, an ISAba13 insertion in a putative glycosyltransferase and a subpopulation-associated frameshift in wzx. AC03 formed plaques on all six strains with capsule-locus changes but on none of the five strains without them. Capsule dependence differed among the other phages: relative to the parental AB5075, infection by these phages, Equilibrator, Taro and BB02, was restricted on the capsule-deficient wzc::T26 strain, whereas AT01 efficiency was only slightly reduced. Insertion-site mapping also distinguished a near-terminal adeK insertion that retained the parental antimicrobial phenotype from an early adeK insertion associated with loss of AdeIJK function. Together, these findings identify capsule-locus variation as the strongest correlation with phage susceptibility in this panel and demonstrate the importance of verifying mutant genomes before assigning phenotypes to their annotated insertions.

papers.title: A Staphylococcus phage recombination cassette that enables recombineering across distant bacteria
papers.abstract: Modifying bacterial genomes with phage recombinases, a process termed recombineering, has enabled precise genome editing, but its reach is limited by host specificity: each new organism generally requires its own recombinase to be identified and optimized. Using known phage recombination genes as synteny anchors, we mined Staphylococcus genomes and recovered a diverse collection of phage recombination cassettes, spanning the RAD52-like annealase superfamily (Sak, Erf) and the RAD51/RecA-like Sak4 family. Functional testing of representatives in S. aureus identified several highly efficient systems that support recombineering. We engineered the most efficient of these into a single-plasmid tool that yields markerless editing in S. aureus in four days. Notably, where other recombineering systems rely on host-specific factors for nuclease evasion and ssDNA loading, this cassette encodes both activities itself: a predicted broad-spectrum nuclease inhibitor and a dedicated single-stranded DNA-binding protein. We therefore tested the cassette across phylogenetically distant hosts, and observed recombination in Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecium, Francisella novicida, and Escherichia coli. These results identify a self-sufficient class of phage recombination systems and provide a portable tool for

papers.title: Higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals gate pathobiont expansion through succinate-driven pH modulation
papers.abstract: Despite advances in defining microbiome shifts associated with inflammatory mucosal diseases, the ecological interactions that constrain or facilitate pathobiont expansion remain poorly understood. Using a six-species synthetic oral microbial community and factorial interaction screening, we identified a higher-order interaction governing the growth of the periodontal pathobiont Porphyromonas gingivalis. The core community member Veillonella parvula was the strongest positive determinant of P. gingivalis growth, but this effect was substantially reduced by the health-associated commensal Actinomyces oris. A. oris-mediated antagonism resulted from extracellular acidification and was enhanced under anaerobic conditions. Genetic dissection of A. oris fermentation revealed that lactate dehydrogenase (ldh1) contributes to anaerobic lactate production, but ldh1 deletion only partially relieved P. gingivalis inhibition. Instead, succinate, produced through a succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase pathway (sdh2), emerged as the principal driver of acidification and P. gingivalis suppression. At high cell densities, however, V. parvula consumed both lactate and succinate, reversing acidification and restoring conditions permissive for P. gingivalis growth. To assess the relevance of these interactions in vivo, we analyzed subgingival microbiome from 1,355 adults, including 555 with detectable P. gingivalis. Among these individuals, P. gingivalis abundance was negatively associated with Actinomyces abundance after adjustment for periodontitis severity, whereas this association was attenuated at high V. parvula abundance, consistent with the interaction observed in vitro. Together, these findings identify succinate as a previously unrecognized mediator of interbacterial antagonism and reveal how higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals regulate pathobiont expansion through pH modulation, with protective effects shaped by oxygen availability and metabolic cross-feeding.

papers.title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
papers.abstract: Background Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus) system comprising free-living mice (Wild:As), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like:As), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like:As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory Mus musculus (Lab-like:As). We compared these three Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory Mus musculus (Lab:Mm) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions. Results We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab:Mm and Lab-like:As than in Wild:As and Wild-like:As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild:As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like:As mice remained most similar to Wild:As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like:As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like:As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab:Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in [≥]90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild:As to 46 in Wild-like:As, 72 in Lab-like:As, and 138 in Lab:Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild:As and Wild-like:As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like:As shifted toward the Lab:Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct. Conclusions Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.
